Parents are afraid of migrant children

Many migrants, many problems? Some mothers and fathers are doing everything so their kids can switch schools

Analysis by Jenny Hoch

It seemed simple. Marie would attend the elementary school nearby, just like the other children in her quarter. Matthias Schubert, her father, didn't mind that the percentage of immigrant population, here in Munich's west, was higher than elsewhere. He didn't want special treatment for his daughter. Many times he made fun of other parents who pretended to their children that all was nice and peachy with the world. He liked the colorful mix in his part of town.

The PTA meeting at school seemed promising. The teachers seemed nice, the principal engaged, the educational program made sense. It just seemed strange to him how many waves the staff made about his daughter. "She seemed to have been elevated into some kind of celebrity status", he says. Soon he realized why. Originally, sixteen children were supposed to start first grade. But one couple after another applied to switch their children to different schools. Marie was the last of the German first graders with "migration background". After pondering the issue for a while, the Schuberts did the same for Marie as the other parents. They applied to switch her to a different school.

It's a clash of ideals that's happening every year in the rapidly changing ethnic quarters of big German cities. German parents who saw themselves as cosmopolitan and tolerant and lived among Turks, Arabs and Eastern Europeans are faced with the dilemma. Send their kid to a school with social problems because that's the fair and socially just thing to do? Or should they send their child to a school that offers her or him the best possible environment for an education? What is a better environment anyway? Maybe it would be better to attend a socially mixed school because it prepares for life in a heterogeneous society?

In these weeks and months, the merry-go-round of finding a place in an elementary school goes into high gear. Theoretically, it's supposed to spin slowly, so everyone, regardless of his origin, can climb aboard. That's why pretty much all over Germany, the parish principle applies, meaning first graders are sent to schools in districts close to where they live. Sounds reasonable. The way to school shouldn't be too far, and social selection at this age should be prevented. In practice, things look different.

Every year, parents refuse to go along with this. In the big cities, around 10% apply to switch their children to different schools, especially Germans who are well educated and a good income. Parents with migratory background decide far less often against the school assigned to their children. The result: social rifts in schools are becoming larger. Schools in "problem districts" with high migrant populations are being avoided, schools in well situated middle class preferred, whether the parents live there or not.

"It was a decision of brain versus heart", confirms Matthias Schubert. And yes, he still feels bad about it. "I'd never thought I'd one time be one of those helicopter parents." But to make his daughter the poster child for integration? He didn't want that. Today she's attending a school with high population of immigrants. But at least not as the only German child. His conclusion: if all parents would work together, this problem wouldn't exist. Switching schools is way too easy."

In fact there are many ways to evade the assigned parish school. If your application to a different school is rejected, you can veto that decision by the school board. "This works most of the time", says a Berlin lawyer who specialized in school law. He checks if the school board made a mistake and fights its decisions.

Another point are fake address registrations. "A big subject", the lawyer says. "There are certain schools where you can guess there's probably 20% of students with faked addresses." He's talking about parents who register themselves as living in a desired school district without living there. He suggests not to do that, because of the danger of getting caught.

If it was up to Kirsten Hinkler, every family could pick and choose which school their children attend. The artist lives with her partner and two sons in Berlin-Schoeneberg. When their older son was to start first grade in 2013, he was assigned to a school with 70% of non-German students. "Nobody from our daycare wanted to go there, everybody said it was horrible there." So she asked if she could sit in through a few classes to see for herself. No can do, sorry! So when it came to filling out the paperwork, almost everybody asked to be assigned to a different school, resulting in the school secretary being extremely rude and obnoxious. Overall, she felt the entire procedure of filling out the applications to start first grade in the school of her liking was extremely unpleasant. "It took months before it became clear which school my son would attend. This uncertainty was bad for him."

In the end, she selected a private Montessori school. "Children there aren't to fulfill the expectations of the teachers, but the teachers are to fulfill the expectations of the children. This attitude convinced me.", Kirsten Hinkler says. Never mind that the school is way out in the boonies and her son had to be delivered and picked up there every day. "Parents organized ride shares right away, no big deal."
